questions.stem: A 19 year old student had a splenectomy after a cycling accident 9 months ago. He has a 10 hour history of fever, headache and a spreading non-blanching rash on his legs. His temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. Blood culture Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gram-negative diplococci with a purpuric rash is meningococcal sepsis, one of the encapsulated organisms asplenic patients cannot clear.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Asplenic + purpura + **Gram-negative diplococci** = **N. meningitidis**.

elim: The commonest cause of OPSI, but a Gram-positive diplococcus.

steps.x: **C. Neisseria meningitidis.** Encapsulated organisms: S. pneumoniae, Klebsiella, H. influenzae, Pseudomonas, N. meningitidis, Cryptococcus.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy who had a splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis has not had any childhood immunisations because his parents declined them. He develops a high fever, drooling and stridor. His temperature is 39.6°C. Blood cultures grow a Gram-negative coccobacillus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Unvaccinated asplenic children are at high risk from Hib, an encapsulated Gram-negative coccobacillus causing epiglottitis and sepsis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Unvaccinated + epiglottitis + **Gram-negative coccobacillus** = **Hib**.

elim: Gram-negative diplococcus and not a cause of epiglottitis in this setting.

steps.x: **A. Haemophilus influenzae type b.** Keep childhood immunisations up to date in asplenia, including Hib.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with alcohol dependence had a splenectomy for trauma 5 years ago. He has a 2 day history of fever, rigors and a cough with thick, dark red 'redcurrant jelly' sputum. His temperature is 39.0°C, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows right upper lobe consolidation (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Klebsiella, an encapsulated Gram-negative rod, causes upper lobe pneumonia with redcurrant jelly sputum in alcohol-dependent and asplenic patients.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Alcohol + asplenia + **redcurrant jelly sputum** = **Klebsiella**.

elim: Atypical with hyponatraemia and diarrhoea; no redcurrant jelly sputum.
Mild atypical illness in young people.
Often follows influenza and causes cavitation, not redcurrant jelly sputum.

steps.x: **A. Klebsiella pneumoniae.** Klebsiella is one of the encapsulated organisms.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with coeliac disease that she manages poorly has had two episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia in a year. Her spleen is not palpable and she has never had abdominal surgery. Her haemoglobin is 112 g/L and platelets 460 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her blood film?
questions.e: Coeliac disease can cause functional hyposplenism; without splenic pitting, nuclear remnants (Howell-Jolly bodies) stay in red cells.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on her blood film? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Coeliac + recurrent pneumococcal infection = **functional hyposplenism**: **Howell-Jolly bodies**.
**B. Howell-Jolly bodies.** Howell-Jolly bodies are the marker of hyposplenism.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman had an elective splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia 10 days ago. She now has a painful, swollen left calf that is 4 cm larger than the right. She is not breathless. Her platelet count, which was 30 × 10⁹/L before surgery, is now 820 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: After splenectomy, surgery and a reactive rise in platelets raise the risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Post-splenectomy **thrombocytosis** + swollen calf = **DVT**.

elim: Follows knee arthritis; the post-operative thrombocytosis points to clotting.
A tender cord along a superficial vein, not a swollen calf.

steps.x: **D. Deep vein thrombosis.** Splenectomy complications: DVT, PE, pneumonia, haemorrhage, sepsis.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man had an emergency splenectomy after a rugby injury 8 hours ago. He now has increasing abdominal pain and distension. His pulse rate is 132 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. His surgical drain has filled with 600 mL of fresh blood. His haemoglobin has fallen from 118 to 76 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Early haemorrhage (often from the splenic vessels) is a recognised complication of splenectomy: hypotension, falling Hb and blood in the drain.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Shock + **fresh blood in drain** + falling Hb hours after surgery = **haemorrhage**.

elim: Too early and no fever; the drain shows bleeding.
Causes amylase-rich drain fluid later, not fresh blood.
Would not explain fresh blood in the drain.
Occurs days later with swinging fever.

steps.x: **A. Intra-abdominal haemorrhage.** Splenectomy complications include haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman is recovering from a splenectomy after a car accident. She has received her vaccinations and is starting penicillin prophylaxis. She asks when she will be at greatest risk of overwhelming infection.
questions.q: When is her risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection greatest?
o: In the first 2 years after splenectomy
questions.e: OPSI risk is greatest in the first two years after splenectomy, though it remains lifelong.

steps.x: The lead-in is: When is her risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection greatest? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
OPSI: **first two years** are highest risk; lifelong risk remains.

elim: Risk persists lifelong but is highest early.
Risk is lower than in the first years.
Risk extends well beyond the post-operative period.
Risk is not age-limited this way.

steps.x: **C. In the first 2 years after splenectomy.** OPSI risk is greatest in the first two years.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl with sickle cell disease has been unwell for 6 hours with a fever of 39.8°C, lethargy and poor feeding. Her pulse rate is 168 bpm and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Her parents have stopped giving her daily penicillin. Blood culture shows Gram-positive diplococci.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Children with sickle cell disease have functional asplenia; pneumococcal sepsis (Gram-positive diplococci) is the commonest and most dangerous infection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Functional asplenia + **Gram-positive diplococci** = **S. pneumoniae**.

elim: Gram-negative rod (Salmonella is linked to osteomyelitis in sickle cell).

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pneumoniae.** Pneumococcal sepsis is the most common serious infection in hyposplenism.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a routine blood test before a hernia repair. Her blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies. She feels well. She was in a car crash 20 years ago and needed an emergency laparotomy. She does not have sickle cell disease or coeliac disease.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the blood film finding?
questions.e: The most common cause of hyposplenism is splenectomy, here after trauma; patients are often asymptomatic.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of the blood film finding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: does not have sickle cell disease
steps.x: Howell-Jolly bodies + **past trauma laparotomy** = likely **splenectomy**.

elim: Causes macrocytosis but does not explain Howell-Jolly bodies in this context.
Gives microcytic, hypochromic cells and pencil cells.
Gives tear-drop cells and a large spleen.

steps.x: **D. Splenectomy.** Splenectomy (trauma or haematological) is the commonest cause.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is on day 3 after an open splenectomy for a splenic tumour. He has a temperature of 38.4°C, cough with green sputum and pain at the left lower chest on deep breathing. His oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air. Breath sounds are reduced at the left base. Chest X-ray shows left lower zone consolidation (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pneumonia, especially at the left base where splinting and atelectasis occur, is a common complication after splenectomy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Post-splenectomy fever + **green sputum + left basal consolidation** = **pneumonia**.

elim: Usually later with swinging fever; X-ray shows consolidation.
Fulminant sepsis with shock, not a localised chest infection.
Would not usually give purulent sputum and focal consolidation.

steps.x: **A. Left lower lobe pneumonia.** Pneumonia is a post-splenectomy complication.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with sickle cell disease is moving to a new haematology service. His spleen is not palpable. The team wants to confirm whether he has functional asplenia before deciding on vaccinations and lifelong prophylaxis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm splenic dysfunction?
questions.e: The blood film is the gold standard: Howell-Jolly bodies show splenic dysfunction.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm splenic dysfunction? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: confirm whether he has functional asplenia
steps.x: **Splenic dysfunction** is confirmed on a **blood film** (Howell-Jolly bodies).

elim: Confirms sickle cell disease, not splenic function.

steps.x: **B. Blood film.** Gold standard: blood film.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man registers with a new GP. He had a splenectomy after a motorbike crash 6 years ago abroad. He is well. He is not sure which vaccines he had afterwards or whether he should be taking any medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial step?
o: Abdominal CT to look for splenic tissue
Full blood count and check his immunisation record
No action as risk has passed
questions.e: First-line work-up in hyposplenism is an FBC and confirmation of immunisation status, so missing vaccines and prophylaxis can be arranged.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial step? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: not sure which vaccines he had
steps.x: Asplenic, unclear history: **FBC + immunisation status**.

elim: He is well and not febrile.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count and check his immunisation record.** First-line: FBC and confirm immunisation status.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman who had a splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis attends the emergency department with 4 hours of fever and rigors. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. There is no obvious source. A cannula has been inserted.
questions.q: Which investigation should be taken immediately, without delaying antibiotics?
questions.e: Fever in an asplenic patient is an emergency: take blood cultures, but immediate IV antibiotics must not be delayed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which investigation should be taken immediately, without delaying antibiotics? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Asplenic + fever = **emergency**: **blood cultures** then **immediate IV antibiotics**.

elim: Not urgent; she is known to be asplenic.
Not first and must not delay antibiotics.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Fever in asplenia is an emergency: cultures and IV antibiotics now.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man had a laparoscopic splenectomy 9 days ago. He has a swollen, tender right calf. He is not breathless and his oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air. His platelet count is 740 × 10⁹/L. His Wells score for DVT is 3.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Post-splenectomy thrombocytosis and surgery raise the risk of DVT; a likely Wells score needs a proximal leg vein ultrasound.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Post-splenectomy **DVT likely** = **leg ultrasound**.

elim: With a likely Wells score, imaging is needed; D-dimer is raised after surgery anyway.

steps.x: **D. Proximal leg vein ultrasound.** Splenectomy complications include DVT and PE.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with type 2 diabetes had a splenectomy 4 years ago. Her HbA1c is repeatedly higher than expected from her home glucose readings, which are mostly 5 to 8 mmol/L. Her diabetes team wants a more accurate measure of control.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess her glycaemic control?
questions.e: After splenectomy red cells live longer and become more glycosylated, so HbA1c reads falsely high; glucose monitoring (or fructosamine) gives a truer picture.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess her glycaemic control? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Post-splenectomy, **HbA1c is falsely raised**: measure glucose directly.
**A. Continuous glucose monitoring.** Longer red cell survival after splenectomy raises HbA1c.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man had an emergency splenectomy for a ruptured spleen after a fall 2 days ago. He had no vaccinations before surgery. He is recovering well and is due to go home in a week.
questions.q: When is the most appropriate time to give his pneumococcal vaccine?
o: Never, as the spleen is gone
Only if he develops an infection
questions.e: For elective splenectomy, pneumococcal vaccine is given 2 weeks before; after emergency splenectomy it is given at least 2 weeks after surgery.

steps.x: The lead-in is: When is the most appropriate time to give his pneumococcal vaccine? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Elective: **2 weeks before**; emergency: **2 weeks after**.

elim: Response is poorer immediately after surgery.
Too long a gap at the highest-risk time.

steps.x: **A. At least 2 weeks after surgery.** Pneumococcal vaccine 2 weeks before elective splenectomy.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman had a splenectomy for trauma 5 years ago. She received her pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccines then and has had an influenza vaccine every autumn. She takes penicillin V daily and asks if she needs any other vaccine now.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate vaccine to give now?
questions.e: Asplenic patients need a pneumococcal booster every 5 years, plus annual influenza.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate vaccine to give now? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: has had an influenza vaccine every autumn
steps.x: Splenectomy **5 years ago** = **pneumococcal booster** due.

elim: She is due her 5-yearly pneumococcal booster.

steps.x: **D. Pneumococcal booster.** 5-yearly pneumococcal booster, annual influenza.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman with hereditary spherocytosis is listed for an elective laparoscopic splenectomy in 4 weeks. She has had all routine childhood vaccines. The surgical team is planning her pre-operative care.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate set of vaccines before surgery?
questions.e: Before elective splenectomy she needs pneumococcal (2 weeks before), Hib and meningococcal vaccines, then annual influenza.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate set of vaccines before surgery? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Asplenia vaccines: **pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal** (+ annual flu).

elim: Elective cases are vaccinated 2 weeks before.

steps.x: **D. Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccines.** Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms before elective splenectomy.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man is being discharged after a splenectomy for trauma. He has had his vaccines and is starting penicillin V. He plans to go travelling next year and asks what else he should do to stay safe.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Seek urgent medical help for any fever and carry an alert card
Stop penicillin when he feels well
Take paracetamol and wait for 3 days if febrile
questions.e: Patients must be educated that fever is an emergency, seek urgent help and carry an alert card.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate advice? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Asplenia education: **fever = emergency**, **alert card**.

elim: Fever is a medical emergency in asplenia.
Vaccines do not cover every organism.

steps.x: **B. Seek urgent medical help for any fever and carry an alert card.** Educate to seek urgent help for fever; carry an alert card.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl has had a splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis. She has had all vaccines. Her parents are told she will take daily phenoxymethylpenicillin and ask how long it must continue.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Lifelong, or at least through the highest-risk period
Only while she has a fever
questions.e: Daily penicillin V protects against S. pneumoniae and is given lifelong, or at least through the highest-risk period, especially in children and early after splenectomy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate advice? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Penicillin V: **lifelong**, especially in **children** and early on.
**A. Lifelong, or at least through the highest-risk period.** Prophylaxis: lifelong or at least the highest-risk period.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man who had a splenectomy 3 years ago attends the emergency department with 3 hours of fever and muscle aches. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. He looks unwell. Blood cultures have just been taken. The registrar suggests waiting for the white cell count before deciding.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Oral paracetamol and review in 4 hours
Wait for the blood culture result
Wait for the CRP and white cell count
questions.e: In an asplenic patient with fever and suspected sepsis, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics are given immediately.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: waiting for the white cell count
steps.x: Asplenic + fever = **immediate IV antibiotics**; do not wait for bloods.

elim: Fever in asplenia is an emergency.

steps.x: **B. Give IV ceftriaxone immediately.** Immediate IV antibiotics if sepsis is suspected in asplenia.

questions.stem: A 14 month old boy with sickle cell disease is reviewed in clinic. He takes daily penicillin V. His parents ask what vaccinations he needs. He has had his immunisations up to his first birthday.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Keep routine childhood immunisations up to date with extra pneumococcal vaccine
Stop penicillin once vaccines are complete
questions.e: Children with functional asplenia from sickle cell disease need routine childhood immunisations kept up to date plus additional pneumococcal protection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate advice? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Functional asplenia: **routine childhood vaccines up to date** + extra pneumococcal.
**C. Keep routine childhood immunisations up to date with extra pneumococcal vaccine.** Ensure routine childhood vaccinations are up to date.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man had a splenectomy for a splenic lymphoma 2 years ago. He had pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccines before surgery and takes penicillin V daily. It is now October and he attends his GP for a medication review. He is well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate vaccination plan from now on?
questions.e: Asplenic patients need annual influenza vaccination (influenza predisposes to secondary pneumococcal sepsis) and 5-yearly pneumococcal boosters.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate vaccination plan from now on? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Asplenia: **annual influenza** + 5-yearly pneumococcal.

elim: BCG is live and not part of asplenia care.
Not part of asplenia care if childhood doses were given.

steps.x: **E. Yearly inactivated influenza vaccine.** Annual influenza vaccine for everyone with asplenia.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman had a splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia 2 years ago. Her blood film now shows target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes. She is well with normal haemoglobin.
questions.q: Which function of the spleen has been lost to explain this blood film?
o: Mechanical filtration of abnormal red cells
Storage of iron for haem synthesis
questions.e: The spleen filters abnormal red cells and removes inclusions; without it, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes circulate.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which function of the spleen has been lost to explain this blood film? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes
steps.x: Abnormal red cells stay in circulation = loss of **mechanical filtration**.

elim: Iron is stored mainly in liver and marrow.

steps.x: **B. Mechanical filtration of abnormal red cells.** The spleen gives mechanical filtration and immunological function.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man who had a splenectomy develops fulminant sepsis from Streptococcus pneumoniae. His antibody levels to most organisms are normal. The microbiologist explains that the organism has a feature that makes it hard to clear without a spleen.
questions.q: Which feature of the organism is most responsible?
questions.e: Encapsulated bacteria resist phagocytosis unless opsonised; the spleen makes opsonising IgM and removes poorly opsonised bacteria, so loss causes fulminant sepsis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which feature of the organism is most responsible? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: hard to clear without a spleen
steps.x: Asplenic risk is from **encapsulated** organisms: the **capsule** resists phagocytosis.

elim: Gram-negative feature; S. pneumoniae is Gram-positive.
Feature of S. aureus and S. pyogenes toxic shock.

steps.x: **D. Polysaccharide capsule resisting phagocytosis.** Spleen: opsonising IgM and phagocytosis of encapsulated bacteria.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who had a splenectomy a year ago calls 111 with 2 hours of fever and shivering. She feels 'not too bad'. The call handler wonders whether she can wait to see her GP tomorrow.
questions.q: Which best explains why she must be seen immediately?
o: Fever always means meningitis after splenectomy
Her penicillin prophylaxis has caused an allergy
OPSI can progress within hours to sepsis with DIC and high mortality
She is likely to have a viral infection
questions.e: OPSI is a rapidly progressive sepsis syndrome, often with DIC, with a high mortality unless treated immediately.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains why she must be seen immediately? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Early **OPSI** can look mild, then rapidly progress to **DIC and death**.

elim: Not always; but sepsis risk is high.
Fever and shivering are not an allergy picture.
Cannot be assumed; risk is bacterial sepsis.

steps.x: **C. OPSI can progress within hours to sepsis with DIC and high mortality.** OPSI: rapid progression, DIC, high mortality.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy has recurrent jaundice and anaemia. His blood film shows spherocytes and the eosin-5-maleimide binding test is reduced. His mother had a splenectomy for the same condition as a child and his maternal grandfather is also affected. A splenectomy is planned.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mode of inheritance?
questions.e: Hereditary spherocytosis, treated with splenectomy, is usually autosomal dominant, affecting each generation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mode of inheritance? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Three affected generations with **spherocytes** = HS, **autosomal dominant**.

elim: Would not usually affect three generations.
Never passed on by males, yet the grandfather passed it to his daughter.
Mother to son is possible, but HS is not X-linked.
Males affected through carrier mothers, but HS is not X-linked.

steps.x: **A. Autosomal dominant.** Hereditary spherocytosis is autosomal dominant; splenectomy is therapeutic.

questions.stem: A newborn baby is diagnosed with sickle cell disease on the heel-prick screen. His parents are told he will start daily penicillin from 2 to 3 months of age, although his spleen will initially be enlarged, not small.
questions.q: Which best explains why he needs penicillin from early infancy?
o: Recurrent splenic infarction causes functional asplenia by early childhood
Sickle cell disease causes low IgG from birth
questions.e: Vaso-occlusion causes repeated splenic infarction, progressive atrophy and autosplenectomy, with functional asplenia evident by early childhood.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains why he needs penicillin from early infancy? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Recurrent splenic infarction** = **functional asplenia** in early childhood.

elim: It is present but progressively destroyed.

steps.x: **B. Recurrent splenic infarction causes functional asplenia by early childhood.** Sickle cell: autosplenectomy by early childhood.
